Financial return (R=(V1​−V0​+D)/V0​)

Words: 54
Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
For initial asset value V0​>0, final value V1​, and intervening cash distribution D, the net financial return is (V1​−V0​+D)/V0​. Its gross return is 1+R=(V1​+D)/V0​. In a one-period portfolio with initial-value weights wi​ summing to one, the net return is ∑i​wi​Ri​. The expected return is its expected value; a realized return need not equal it.

Financial market

Words: 45
Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
A model specifying traded financial assets, their price and payment processes, available information, and allowed admissible trading strategies. A self-financing portfolio generates wealth using gains on these assets. Absence of arbitrage and market completeness respectively concern whether trading can create a riskless profit from zero capital and whether every specified contingent claim can be replicated.

Financial asset

Words: 626 Articles: 9
Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
A traded claim or instrument carrying a current price and future payments or resale value. In a one-period financial market, its terminal payoff is a random variable and a portfolio combines payoffs linearly through its asset holdings. A stock, a zero-coupon bond and a bank account are basic examples. Dividends require treating the full gain process rather than only resale prices.

Credit derivative

Words: 518 Articles: 7
Financial asset OurBigBook.com
A credit derivative transfers exposure to deterioration of credit quality or a specified credit event of a reference borrower without necessarily transferring the underlying loan or bond. Credit default swaps transfer a defined loss exposure; total return swaps transfer a wider asset return. Funded structures such as credit-linked notes combine the exposure with an investor's initial principal. Documentation specifies the reference entity, obligations, credit events and settlement; a hedge can leave counterparty credit risk and mismatch with the original exposure.

Synthetic CDO

Words: 128 Articles: 1
Credit derivative OurBigBook.com
A synthetic collateralized debt obligation creates portfolio credit exposure using credit default swaps rather than necessarily owning a pool of cash loans or bonds. Losses are allocated to tranches with different attachment and exhaustion levels. A tranche can be funded, unfunded or partly funded depending on structure. Individual default probabilities alone do not price it: dependence among defaults and recovery outcomes changes the portfolio loss distribution.
Credit tranche loss function (ℓA,D​(L)=min((L−A)+,D−A))
Words: 72
Synthetic CDO OurBigBook.com
For aggregate monetary loss L and monetary attachment/exhaustion levels A<D, this is the loss allocated to the tranche. It is zero until attachment, rises with losses between A and D, and is capped at D−A. Expected tranche losses and surviving tranche notional determine protection and premium legs. For basket products whose payoff occurs at a first default, the joint default-time distribution matters as well as the final loss distribution.

Credit-linked note

Words: 64
Credit derivative OurBigBook.com
A funded note whose coupons or principal depend on specified credit events of a reference entity or portfolio. In a simple structure, the investor supplies principal and receives enhanced coupon for economically selling credit protection; a reference default reduces principal repayment. The investor may also face the note issuer's own credit risk. This is not automatically the same exposure as directly holding the reference borrower's bond.

Total return swap (asset income and price change ↔ funding leg)

Words: 60
Credit derivative OurBigBook.com
The total-return receiver obtains a reference asset's income and price gains, pays its price losses, and pays an agreed funding leg to the total-return payer. This supplies economic exposure without buying the reference asset outright. The transfer includes ordinary market-price risk as well as credit risk, distinguishing it from a credit default swap. Both parties can have counterparty credit risk as the swap's replacement value changes.

Credit default swap (premium payments ↔ N(1−R) at default)

Words: 199 Articles: 2
Credit derivative OurBigBook.com
The protection buyer pays a contractual premium in exchange for compensation upon a defined credit event of the reference entity. In a simple cash-settled contract of notional N, a default loss with fractional recovery R gives payment N(1−R). Physical settlement instead exchanges an eligible defaulted obligation for par. Payments, accrued premium, maturity and eligible obligations depend on the contract. The protection buyer need not own the reference debt; the seller earns premium while taking the specified credit risk.
First-to-default swap (τfirst​=mini​τi​)
Words: 55
Credit default swap OurBigBook.com
A basket credit contract whose protection payment is triggered by the first specified default among its reference entities. The loss and settlement terms refer to the defaulting name according to the contract. Premium generally stops at that first default or maturity. Pricing requires the joint default-time distribution; separate marginal default probabilities alone do not determine the first-default law.
Continuous-premium credit-default swap spread (s=(1−R)∫0T​B(t)G(t)dt∫0T​B(t)λ(t)G(t)dt​)
Words: 64
Credit default swap OurBigBook.com
Assume deterministic discount factors, deterministic risk-neutral default intensity λ, fixed fractional recovery R, and continuous premium until default or maturity. Survival is G(t)=exp(−∫0t​λ(u)du). Expected discounted protection is N(1−R)∫BλG, while premium is Ns∫BG. Equating them gives the par spread. Constant intensity gives s=(1−R)λ. Discrete premiums, default accrual, stochastic recovery and counterparty losses require changing the corresponding cash-flow expectations.

Risk-free asset (R=1/B)

Words: 55
Financial asset OurBigBook.com
For a fixed horizon, a risk-free asset has a deterministic terminal payoff. If the price of a unit terminal payoff is B>0, its gross return is R=1/B. In a finite state market, the sum of the Arrow state prices is B. Risk-free does not mean that a longer-maturity bond has a deterministic resale price before its maturity.

With only local martingale prices and a lower-bound restriction on admissible trading strategies, it can fail: the seemingly profitable short position may have unbounded possible losses before maturity.

Let Y be the discounted gains of finitely many financial assets on any probability space. Conversely, under such a measure a nonnegative terminal gain with zero initial price has zero expectation, and must vanish almost surely. In an arbitrage-free one-period market with finitely many assets and an equivalent martingale measure, market completeness is equivalent to uniqueness of the dominated martingale measure. Completeness prices every indicator function, forcing two measures to agree on every event. Conversely, if the attainable payoff span has dimension k but is not the whole payoff space, choose k+1 disjoint positive-probability events. Their moment vectors against a basis of attainable payoffs are linearly dependent. A nonzero bounded linear combination h of their indicators consequently has zero pricing moments. Multiplying an existing equivalent density by 1+εh, for sufficiently small positive and negative ε, constructs distinct equivalent martingale measures. This proves the converse without assuming that the original space was finite. On a general probability space, completeness here means replication of all bounded claims, or equivalently all square-integrable claims when asset payoffs are square-integrable.

A smooth value function satisfying the Black-Scholes equation admits a self-financing portfolio with the displayed delta hedge. An arbitrary decomposition p=xg+Bh need not be self-financing. For example p=0, g=1, h=−x/B solves the value equation but has portfolio gains dS−ρSdt, which are not zero when volatility is positive. For specified holdings, self-financing is equivalent to the value equation together with g=px​.

Greeks (finance)

Words: 361 Articles: 5
Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
The Greeks are sensitivities of a financial claim value to model inputs, expressed through partial derivatives. The option delta measures sensitivity to the underlying price; a delta hedge uses that sensitivity to cancel first-order price exposure.

Option theta (Θ=∂t​V)

Words: 91
Greeks (finance) OurBigBook.com
The derivative of an option's value with respect to calendar time at fixed current underlying price and other parameters. In the dividend-free Black-Scholes model, the Black-Scholes equation gives
Θ=ρ(V−xVx​)−21​σ2x2Vxx​.
(49)
The first term is the interest earned on the bond value of the replicating portfolio, while the second uses option gamma. A convex payoff with a short bond position has Θ≤0 when ρ≥0; a concave payoff with a long bond position has Θ≥0. Negative interest rates need not obey these signs: the affine payoff x−K has Θ=−ρKe−ρ(T−t). For a fixed payoff function, remaining-maturity sensitivity is −Θ.

Option delta (Δ)

Words: 239 Articles: 3
Greeks (finance) OurBigBook.com
The option delta is the derivative of an option value with respect to the underlying asset price. In a smooth complete diffusion model, it is also the number of underlying units in the replicating delta hedge.

Delta hedge (Δ=∂s​V)

Words: 36
Option delta OurBigBook.com
A delta hedge holds Δt​=∂s​V(t,St​) units of the risky asset. In the Black-Scholes model, this choice cancels the claim's Brownian exposure.
The option delta is one of the Greeks (finance); hedging is the trading procedure that uses this sensitivity.

Call delta equation for a driftless local volatility diffusion (U=VS​)

Words: 168 Articles: 1
Option delta OurBigBook.com
In the cash-numéraire market dSt​=a(St​)dWt​, let a smooth call value solve Vt​+21​a2VSS​=0. Its delta hedge is U=VS​. Differentiating the pricing equation gives
Ut​+aa′US​+21​a2USS​=0,U(T,S)=1{S≥K}​,
(50)
with the terminal value at the strike understood up to the null probability of the diffusion hitting that exact terminal value. By Itô formula, dU(t,St​)=−aa′US​dt+aUS​dWt​, while dV(t,St​)=U(t,St​)dSt​. Thus holding U(t,St​) shares and cash V−SU replicates the terminal call. The drift in the option delta equation comes from differentiating the spatially varying diffusion coefficient, not from a drift in the original stock.
Derivative-weighted call delta martingale (Mt​=Zt​πt​)
Words: 82
Call delta equation for a driftless local volatility diffusion OurBigBook.com
Suppose a′ is bounded and let dZt​=Zt​a′(St​)dWt​, Z0​=1. The Novikov condition makes Z a strictly positive true martingale. For πt​=U(t,St​) solving the call delta equation for a driftless local volatility diffusion, the product formula gives
d(Zt​πt​)=Zt​(a(St​)US​(t,St​)+a′(St​)U(t,St​))dWt​.
(51)
The two drift terms cancel through quadratic covariation. Thus Zπ is a local martingale. If it is a true martingale on the closed horizon, its terminal value is ZT​1{ST​≥K}​, so
πt​=Zt​E[ZT​1{ST​≥K}​∣Ft​]​,0≤πt​≤1.
(52)
The upper bound uses E[ZT​∣Ft​]=Zt​. Equivalently, the option delta is the terminal-exceedance probability under the measure with density ZT​.

Implied volatility is the volatility input of an option-pricing model that reproduces an observed option price. Black-Scholes implied volatility specializes this inversion to the Black-Scholes model.

The Black-Scholes implied volatility is the volatility parameter that makes the Black-Scholes price equal an observed claim price.

American option

Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
An American option may be exercised at any time up to maturity. Its value is the Snell envelope of its discounted exercise payoff.

American call option (supτ≤T​EQ​[e−∫tτ​rs​ds(Sτ​−X)+])

Words: 210 Articles: 2
American option OurBigBook.com
An American call permits purchase of the underlying at strike X at a chosen stopping time no later than maturity. Under standard pricing and integrability hypotheses its value is the displayed optimal stopping value. A European call option restricts exercise to the final time. Dividends and interest on the deferred strike affect the incentive to exercise early.

Dividend-date call-exercise criterion (D<X(1−B(t1​,T)))

Words: 77
American call option OurBigBook.com
For a single known cash dividend at t1​, nonnegative interest excludes exercise strictly before the last cum-dividend opportunity. Immediately before the dividend, continuation has lower bound St1​−​−D−XB(t1​,T), whereas positive immediate exercise pays St1​−​−X. The displayed inequality makes continuation strictly better. With no further dividends, it therefore excludes all early exercise. If the inequality fails, exercise just before the dividend may be worthwhile, but is not automatically optimal because remaining option time value also matters.

No early exercise of a call without dividends

Words: 83
American call option OurBigBook.com
For a non-dividend-paying stock and nonnegative deterministic interest, the European call lower bound is CE​≥S−XB, where B≤1 is the zero-coupon bond price. This is at least the in-the-money exercise payoff S−X; the call also preserves the possibility of avoiding payment of the strike. Positive interest makes the comparison strict when exercise would have positive payoff. At zero interest there can be indifference, and with negative interest the statement can fail: a deterministic stock Su​=S0​eru with r<0 can give a larger payoff by immediate exercise.

Words: 80
American option OurBigBook.com
In a discrete-time binomial market with Bt​=(1+r)t and one-step stock factors 1±ε, use the risk-neutral probability p=(1+r/ε)/2, where 0≤r<ε<1. For the exercise payoff St2​, the discounted one-step reward multiplier has mean
λ=1+r1+2r+ε2​>1.
(53)
The Snell envelope of a multiplicative process gives the value Vt​=St2​λT−t. Continuation strictly exceeds exercise before maturity, so the optimal exercise time is T. The replicating portfolio in a binomial market holds 2St​λT−t−1 shares on the next step, found by subtracting the two next-state values and dividing by the stock-price difference. At time zero the price is S02​λT.

For payoff g(s)=(1+s)−1 and α=2r/σ2∈(0,1), the exercise boundary is b=α/(1−α). The value equals g below b and (1+b)−1(s/b)−α above it. Value matching, smooth fit, and the obstacle problem verify the first down-crossing policy.

If a nonnegative value V dominates the payoff and a=rV−Lr​V≥0, delta holdings V′(S) combined with a reserve satisfying dD=(rD+a(S))dt give a self-financing portfolio of wealth V(S)+D. The reserve retains the surplus instead of consuming it, so the wealth dominates the payoff at every exercise time.

Modern portfolio theory

Words: 450 Articles: 8
Mathematical finance OurBigBook.com
Mean-variance optimization balances expected linear return against a positive-definite quadratic variance penalty.
Modern portfolio theory constructs portfolios by comparing expected return with variance risk and the effects of diversification.

Portfolio opportunity set ({(wTΣw​,wTμ):1Tw=1})

Words: 55
Modern portfolio theory OurBigBook.com
The set of attainable return standard deviations and expected returns for budget-feasible risky investment portfolios. Negative weights are allowed when short selling is permitted. With positive definite covariance matrix and nonconstant means, the minimum-risk boundary is a hyperbola in standard-deviation/mean coordinates; its upper branch is the mean-variance efficient frontier. Adding a risk-free asset changes the budget constraint on risky holdings and produces a different attainable set.

Gaussian two-fund theorem

Words: 93
Modern portfolio theory OurBigBook.com
For nondegenerate Gaussian terminal prices, a finite maximizer of a differentiable increasing concave non-affine utility, subject to a linear budget, lies in the span of V−1s and V−1μ. Gaussian integration by parts gives
E[SU′(πTS)]=μEU′(πTS)+VπEU′′(πTS).
(54)
The budget first-order condition makes this a multiple of s. For a nonzero portfolio, non-affineness and the full Gaussian support imply EU′′<0, so rearrangement gives the span assertion. Affine utility is a genuine exception: when means are proportional to prices, every budget-feasible portfolio is optimal, including portfolios outside that span.

Efficient frontier (vmin​(m)=x2/A+(A/D)(m−Bx/A)2)

Words: 104
Modern portfolio theory OurBigBook.com
With fixed budget sTπ=x, positive definite covariance V, and mean vector μ independent of s, set A=sTV−1s, B=sTV−1μ, C=μTV−1μ and D=AC−B2>0. The minimum variance at mean m is the displayed parabola. Its upper-mean branch m≥Bx/A is efficient: the lower branch has a competitor with equal variance and higher mean. If μ is proportional to s, only one mean is feasible and this two-dimensional parabola degenerates.
The efficient frontier is the set of portfolios for which no other feasible portfolio has at least as much expected return and no greater variance, with at least one strict improvement.

Gaussian one-fund theorem

Words: 75
Modern portfolio theory OurBigBook.com
Let ξ∼N(b,Σ), where b=0 and Σ is positive definite. For any increasing concave objective of m+θTξ, every unique optimal portfolio has the form
θ∗=λΣ−1b,λ≥0.
(56)
Indeed, the component orthogonal to Σ−1b in the Σ inner product contributes independent mean-zero Gaussian risk without changing the mean. Removing it cannot reduce expected concave utility. A negative coefficient is dominated by the corresponding positive coefficient, which has the same variance and a larger mean.
